papers.title: Postoperative fluid collection at the proximal neurovascular bundle level is associated with early pain and reduced knee extensor strength after direct anterior total hip arthroplasty
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Early anterolateral thigh pain after direct anterior total hip arthroplasty (DAA-THA) is common, and more severe symptoms than expected in the usual postoperative course can be difficult to interpret clinically. This study evaluated whether a landmark-based ultrasonographic pattern of postoperative fluid collection (POFC) at a reference level corresponding to a reported course of the proximal neurovascular bundle is associated with early pain and knee extensor strength. Methods In this prospective cohort study, ultrasonography was performed at 1 week postoperatively in 182 patients (182 hips) who underwent DAA-THA. At a prespecified reference cross-section corresponding to a reported level where the proximal neurovascular bundle crosses the femoral midline, POFC extending medially beyond the femoral midline was classified as a midline-crossing POFC. Co-primary outcomes were proximal anterolateral thigh pain while walking, assessed using a numerical rating scale, and knee extension torque at 1 week. P -values for the co-primary outcomes were Holm-adjusted. The Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) subscales were analyzed longitudinally. Results Of the 182 hips, 37 were classified as midline-crossing POFC and 145 as non–midline-crossing POFC. Compared with the non–midline-crossing group, the midline-crossing group had greater proximal anterolateral thigh pain during walking (adjusted mean difference, 3.35 points; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.88–3.81; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and lower knee extension torque (adjusted mean difference, − 0.31 Nm/kg; 95% CI, − 0.38 to − 0.24; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). WOMAC pain scores showed a significant group-by-time interaction. Conclusions Midline-crossing POFC at 1 week after DAA-THA was associated with greater early walking pain and lower knee extensor strength. Ultrasound assessment at this reference level may provide useful adjunctive clinical information for selected patients whose early postoperative anterolateral thigh pain and reduced knee extensor performance appear greater than expected.

papers.title: Engineered organoid platforms for drug delivery evaluation.
papers.abstract: Advanced biomaterials and drug delivery systems (DDSs) require human-relevant models that can capture tissue heterogeneity, physiological barriers, and patient-specific therapeutic responses. Conventional two-dimensional cultures and animal models often fail to reproduce these features, contributing to discrepancies between preclinical evaluation and clinical outcomes. Organoids offer three-dimensional, multicellular platforms that partially recapitulate the architecture and functions of human tissues and therefore provide new opportunities for evaluation of material-tissue interactions. This review first outlines the major types of organoids derived from adult stem cells, pluripotent stem cells, and patient tissues. It then discusses engineering strategies, particularly organoid-on-a-chip systems and 3D bioprinting, that introduce controlled fluid flow, mechanical cues, tissue interfaces, and spatial organization to improve physiological relevance, reproducibility, and screening compatibility. Particular emphasis is placed on the emerging use of organoids for assessing DDSs, including tissue penetration, cellular uptake, transport across mucus and blood-brain barrier models, targeting specificity, therapeutic efficacy, and nanomaterial-associated toxicity. Finally, we examine current challenges, including model standardization, vascularization, immune and stromal integration, quantitative validation, scalability, reproducibility, and cost. Integration with defined biomaterials, microfluidics, automated manufacturing, real-time sensing, and computational analysis may establish organoids as complementary and increasingly predictive platforms for biomaterial evaluation, DDS development, safety assessment, and personalized therapy.

papers.title: DreamLander: A 6-DOF World Model based Reinforcement Learning Planetary Lander
papers.abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.

summary_en.result: The approach achieves landings within 2 meters of the target zone with velocity norm below 0.3 m/s while remaining generalizable across scenarios.
summary_en.validation: Performance is demonstrated through simulation of a 6-DOF entry-descent-landing scenario.

papers.title: Simulating Vein Compressibility for Ultrasound-Guided Femoral Access: Speed, Accuracy, and Phantom Validation
papers.abstract: In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.

summary_en.result: Artery predictions stayed within five percentage points at all depths, vein predictions within three points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press, and solver time per frame dropped by a factor of 976 with only 1.03 points of accuracy loss.

papers.title: Adaptive Output Regulation of Linear Systems with Unknown Harmonic Exosystems and Additive Noise
papers.abstract: This paper addresses error-feedback output regulation for known multivariable linear plants subject to an unknown exosystem and additive Gaussian process and measurement noise. The exosystem generates constant and sinusoidal signals, but its dimension, frequencies, and coupling matrices are unavailable. An output-injection transformation represents the external action through known channels. A causal observer then produces a residual independent of the applied input, whose filtered output separates into a harmonic signal, stationary colored Gaussian noise, and a decaying transient. Using this observation model, a Fourier procedure consistently identifies the number and values of the active positive frequencies in the presence of noise. The identified frequencies determine a regulator through interpolation with stable residual filters. A contractive filter realization, nonexpansive state resizing, and bounded gain updates ensure closed-loop moment bounds uniformly over the selected filter orders. If the gain bound contains the ideal interpolation gain, the adaptive plant response and tracking error converge in mean square to those of the corresponding known-frequency regulator. The limiting mean-square tracking error is a linear function of the process- and measurement-noise covariances. In the absence of both noises, the tracking error converges to zero.

papers.title: $Σ$-LeWM: Learning World Models via S-Information for Robot Control
papers.abstract: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. While early world model architectures relied on decoders to prevent mode collapse and learn a predictable latent space, recent works on world models, such as Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture or LeWorldModel, increasingly aim to learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, utilising only a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term. In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.

papers.title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
papers.abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.

papers.title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.

papers.title: Certify, Report, or Refuse: Harm-Constrained Conformal Prediction for Clinical Actions
papers.abstract: Routing a melanoma case to routine follow-up is a serious action error that diagnostic coverage alone does not rule out. We present Harm-Constrained Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (HC-ROCP), a training-free framework that uses frozen classifier probabilities and adds a harm penalty when choosing prediction sets and actions. We test the resulting policies on disjoint calibration splits with multiplicity adjustment. HC-ROCP certifies supported claims, reports descriptive fallback policies, and refuses unsupported subgroup claims. We evaluate these outputs retrospectively on COVID-19 radiographs, ISIC 2019 dermoscopy, and EyePACS-to-APTOS retinopathy transfer. Across ten calibration seeds, HC-ROCP reduces COVID-19 severe-action errors from the exact risk-optimal baseline's 4.68\% to 0.54\%. At a 5\% budget, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC, but the rare squamous-cell-carcinoma claim is refused. At 1\%, all settings receive descriptive reports. For each budget, we also report the minimum severe-case count needed to pass the global harm gate with zero errors, providing a starting point for further data collection.

papers.title: Shape Holomorphy of the Calderón Projector on Lipschitz Surfaces: Frequency-Explicit Bounds for the Helmholtz
papers.abstract: We establish the holomorphic dependence of the Calderón projector for the Helmholtz operator upon shape boundary deformations of a family of bounded Lipschitz domains in two and three spatial dimensions, with bounds explicit in the wavenumber and the size of the holomorphic extension. More precisely, after transporting the four boundary integral operators contained in the Calderón projector to a fixed reference boundary, we prove that the resulting parameter-to-operator maps admit bounded holomorphic extensions in their natural fractional Sobolev spaces. Unlike approaches that require boundary regularity of class $\mathscr C^{1,1}$ or higher, our argument traces the holomorphic dependence on the shape by transferring elliptic estimates to the boundary through the fundamental solution and the Dirichlet and conormal trace operators. This construction is the key step that allows us to treat Lipschitz-regular boundary deformations.   Furthermore, we show that the domain of holomorphy can be chosen independently of the wavenumber $κ$, while the operator bounds in the corresponding fractional Sobolev spaces contain algebraic factors in $κ$ multiplied by $\exp(Cκδ)$. In particular, for real domains, corresponding to $δ=0$, our single layer estimate recovers, to our knowledge, the best available frequency dependence on general Lipschitz boundaries. For the double layer, adjoint double layer, and hypersingular operators, we obtain novel frequency-explicit bounds.   The results proved in this work provide the analytic foundation for frequency-explicit uncertainty quantification, model order reduction, and high-dimensional approximation of boundary integral operators, their Galerkin discretizations, and the resulting boundary densities and quantities of interest on families of parametrically varying boundaries.

papers.title: Simulation-aided Reinforcement Learning with Control Variates
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms often rely on data collected from a target environment, which can be expensive and noisy. Although simulators can generate large amounts of additional data, standard simulation mixing approaches, which directly combine simulated and real experience, can degrade performance due to simulator inaccuracies, especially when they bias the solution away from the optimal policy. We propose a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, where simulated data is used solely to reduce variance in the learning process rather than directly shaping the learning target. We develop our approach for Policy-Evaluation, which is a fundamental building block of RL algorithms. Then we combine it within the actor-critic framework towards policy improvement, as well as extend it towards offline RL scenarios. Experiments on multiple MuJoCo benchmark tasks demonstrate improvements over standard simulation mixing approaches, highlighting control variates as an effective tool for simulation-aided reinforcement learning.

papers.title: TRACE: Adaptive Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for Open-Ended Molecular Design
papers.abstract: Optimizing molecules under small evaluation budgets requires deciding both where in chemical space to search and which candidate within that region to evaluate. We introduce Trust Region Adaptive Chemical Exploration (TRACE), a framework for open-ended molecular Bayesian optimization (BO), where candidates are generated on demand rather than selected from a fixed library. TRACE combines an objective-free graph-perturbation mechanism with a fixed, chemistry-aware Gaussian process (GP) surrogate using fragprints, a representation combining molecular fingerprints and fragment descriptors. Rather than learning the search geometry itself, TRACE makes the scale of chemical exploration explicit through a Tanimoto-similarity threshold controlling chemical extent and a cardinality budget controlling candidate-search breadth. A simple success/failure controller expands or contracts both quantities during optimization, while the GP and acquisition function select which admissible molecules to evaluate. Across six challenging molecular optimization benchmarks under matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE achieves the strongest overall sample efficiency as measured by the best molecule found as evaluations accumulate. Crossed ablations on two objectives further show that adaptive region control contributes beyond the proposal mechanism, while its benefit depends on the proposal distribution. We further apply TRACE to the stability of iron phthalocyanine (FePc), a non-precious molecular electrocatalyst whose degradation can involve loss of the Fe center. Using a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) workflow designed for accurate energy evaluation, TRACE increases the computed thermodynamic resistance to Fe dissolution from 0.42 to 2.59 eV over 80 designed evaluations.

papers.title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.

papers.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks in the small-data regime: A controlled comparison with classical PDE surrogates
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates for engineering models are often trained on large collections of simulated solutions. We investigate whether physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can achieve accurate predictions from scarce labelled observations by incorporating governing equations and prescribed initial and boundary conditions. We introduce hierarchical loss weighting (H-PINN) and its gradient-direction-aware extension (HO-PINN), which adjust the emphasis on physical constraints according to higher-priority losses. Hierarchical PINNs are compared with Vanilla PINN, tuned gradient boosting, support-vector regression, and Gaussian-process regression on a heat equation and three heterogeneous two-phase-flow benchmarks. Experiments use 20--1000 labelled states and ten paired seeds. Each label is one coordinate--state observation, not a complete simulation. At least one PINN variant achieves the highest mean primary-target \(R^2\) in each interpolation and equation-assisted forecasting comparison at 20 and 50 labels. The advantage for water saturation persists across all tested budgets. Hierarchical weighting reduces variability across runs in selected settings. These results demonstrate that known physics can support accurate neural surrogate predictions from very few solution observations, at substantially higher fitting cost than the tested classical regressors.

papers.title: PhysOPSD: Code as Privilege for Physically Plausible Video Generation
papers.abstract: While modern video generative models achieve remarkable visual fidelity, they remain noticeably brittle when generating physically plausible dynamics and complex interactions. Targeted post-training is crucial, yet supervised fine-tuning suffers from offline state mismatch, and reinforcement learning is hindered by sparse, ill-defined physical reward functions. On-Policy (Self-)Distillation (OPSD) reconciles on-policy rollouts with dense corrective feedback, shifting the core challenge to designing effective privileged context. However, conventional modalities fall short: text prompts are inherently declarative, whereas real reference videos heavily entangle physical laws with visual appearance without parametric control. To this end, we propose PhysOPSD, introducing executable code as privileged physical context for video generation. Unlike static visual observations, executable code instantiates an editable physical world with intrinsic abstraction and controllability. Powered by PhysOPSD-Engine, we translate real-world physical scenarios into verifiable simulation programs. PhysOPSD then incorporates (i) dual-level physical privilege to bridge the information gap via an intermediate bottleneck, alongside (ii) controlled physical variations under shared rollout noise to expose causal dynamic shifts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PhysOPSD substantially improves physical plausibility across diverse backbones, outperforming SFT and RL baselines with only $3$K samples, while preserving general video generation quality.

papers.title: QCC-WM: Linking Macro-State Dynamics and Visual Generation via Quotient Causal Construction
papers.abstract: A key challenge in action-conditioned world modeling is to construct macro-states from high-dimensional observations that support recursive prediction under actions, while keeping their predicted evolution consistent with visual changes in generated observations. We propose QCC-WM, a visual world model based on Quotient-based Causal Construction. QCC-WM uses action responses to guide macro-variable construction for recursive action-conditioned prediction. A shared reference quotient measurement constrains the consistency between predicted states and observed changes, allowing macro-level predictions to provide structured constraints for future visual generation.   Using translational and rotational actions and their predicted responses, the model aggregates local visual features into macro-nodes with spatial correspondence through causal abstraction, and recursively predicts node content and motion under a shared reference measurement. Macro-level predictions guide future observation generation, while predicted motion transports historical appearance information. Node-level errors between generated observations and macro-level targets are then mapped back to the corresponding spatial regions for correction, improving consistency between visual generation and macro-level predictions.   On the US-VLA dataset, QCC-WM achieves an ROI-MSE of 0.01861 for four-step prediction. Compared with the best baseline at each prediction horizon, it reduces LPIPS by 48.59%, 41.68%, and 30.23% for four-step prediction and eight- and sixteen-step recursive extrapolation, respectively. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses show that motion-guided reference transport mainly improves pixel reconstruction, while node-level error feedback further improves perceptual quality and consistency between generated observations and macro-level predictions.

papers.title: How Many Exposures Does a World Model Need? Learning Unseen Game Mechanics at Test Time
papers.abstract: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.

papers.title: A Game-Theoretic MPC Planner for Cooperative and Adversarial Drone Coordination
papers.abstract: We present and evaluate a game-theoretic model predictive control planner for cooperative goal reaching and adversarial pursuit-evasion with drones. The planner combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints and trajectory-tracking interfaces. A comparison of cooperative game solvers assesses their ability to find feasible trajectories that resolve conflicts. A computational study quantifies how number of drones, prediction horizon and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance. Move blocking holds control inputs constant over groups of prediction steps, reducing the number of independent control variables and lowering computation time. Timing measurements identify the practical limits of real-time planning in the tested configurations. PyBullet simulations demonstrate cooperative goal reaching and pursuit-evasion. A laboratory flight complements the simulations by validating the trajectory-tracking interfaces on physical drones. The planner can serve as a basis for further evaluation and controller development.

papers.title: Graph-Based RL for Sequential Rendezvous Planning with Multiple Patrolling USVs
papers.abstract: In patrol missions involving multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs), a designated command USV can support fleet management by sequentially rendezvousing with each patrolling USV. These operations require motion-feasible route planning and priority-aware rendezvous sequencing, with the objective of minimizing mission completion time and total tardiness relative to priority-dependent due dates. We propose a framework combining grid-based path planning, surrogate travel-time prediction, and graph-based reinforcement learning. The path planner accounts for ocean currents and approximates turn-rate constraints through multi-stage maneuvers, with path feasibility empirically validated through trajectory-tracking simulations. For rendezvous sequencing, a Feasible Transition Graph (FTG) represents candidate rendezvous events and temporally feasible transitions, enabling a graph neural network to exploit spatiotemporal rendezvous relationships for policy learning. A surrogate predicts travel times from compact current and motion features to avoid repeated path searches during FTG construction and policy training. Evaluation using grid-based path planning shows statistically significant average objective reductions of 10.5%, 3.5%, and 1.5% compared with greedy, MLP-RL, and 2-step lookahead greedy, respectively. The policy achieves these improvements while requiring approximately 1/35 of the latter's computation time. It maintains its advantage over MLP-RL under unseen priority-tier settings, with larger gains as fleet size increases.

papers.title: Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next
papers.abstract: A sparse terminal reward tells an agent little about its steps. Much of the missing information is implicit in the environment's dynamics, because each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. A world model trained on real transitions can learn to predict what each action changes, but a predicted observation does not by itself show whether success has become more likely. With a binary terminal reward, PPO's critic makes this judgment by estimating the current policy's probability of success, but only for states the agent reaches. Our method, WM-PPO, elegantly brings the two together. For each action the policy samples, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic values the predicted successor. In the policy channel, comparisons among these values give the policy auxiliary advantages; in the value channel, their mean gives the critic an auxiliary target. A shared gate weights both channels according to how reliably comparisons with similar margins predicted real outcomes earlier in training. The policy, critic and world model all learn from the agent's own interaction, with no teacher or privileged information, and only the policy is used at inference. With a comparable number of real environment steps, WM-PPO raises success from PPO's 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. The trained policy more often completes prerequisite steps before placing an object or committing to an answer.

papers.title: Misorientations in dislocation cell structures: Modelling and statistical analysis
papers.abstract: Dislocation pattern formation is accompanied by the emergence of lattice rotations and concomitant misorientations across dislocation walls (cell boundaries). Recent advances in mesoscopic modelling of dislocation patterns enable for the first time a systematic simulation study of this phenomenon. We present simulation results for lattice rotation and misorientation patterns in crystals with face-centered cubic and rocksalt lattice structure. Statistical analysis of the orientation changes across cell walls reveals a transition associated with a symmetry-breaking bifurcation in slip system activity: Below the bifurcation, statistical tests indicate the presence of a single population of misoriented walls whereas, above the bifurcation, two sub-populations of 'incidental' and 'geometrically necessary' dislocation walls are present. Our data analytic approach demonstrates that this distinction does not require prior image segmentation and emphasizes the statistical robustness of the distinction between two types of dislocation walls.

papers.title: A Black-Box Reduction from Regret to Multi-Level Coverage
papers.abstract: Online Conformal Prediction (OCP) sequentially constructs prediction sets whose average empirical coverage converges to a target level over time, for arbitrary, potentially adversarial datasets. In the multi-level setting, prediction sets are produced at $d$ coverage levels at once. Prior work argued for the use of online gradient descent with isotonic projections, which produces sets nested across levels, but with a $\sqrt{d}$ dependence in the per-level coverage convergence rate. Here, we both generalize and improve prior work. First, we show that isotonic projections can be used for the construction of multi-level online conformal prediction sets from \emph{any} online learning algorithm (not just gradient descent). Then, through a black-box reduction, we show that the linearized regret of the online algorithm itself automatically gives control over both per-level coverage and distributional consistency of multi-level predictions via Fenchel duality. Finally, by using the Weighted Interval Score, a standard scoring rule for assessing multi-level interval forecasts, we prove that these projections reduce both the size of the sets and their under-coverage. We study two instantiations of our theory, $p$-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods, both improving the dependence on the number of levels to $\sqrt{\log d}$ for the multi-level OCP problem. Experiments on several datasets show favorable performance compared to baselines.

papers.title: Parametric spatio-temporal reduced-order modelling via Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition and Gaussian Process Regression
papers.abstract: We present SPOD-GPR, a non-intrusive, parametric, spatio-temporal reduced-order model (ROM) that combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), Spectral POD (SPOD), and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). A parametric POD first projects the high-dimensional state onto a low-dimensional subspace. The reduced trajectories are then divided into windowed sections, transformed into the frequency domain, and truncated to the most energetic frequencies. SPOD is then performed independently at each retained frequency, yielding temporally coherent modes and coefficients. The parametric dependence of the POD and SPOD bases is modelled by GPR on a local chart of the Grassmann manifold after Procrustes alignment. The SPOD modal coefficients are learned both as explicit functions of the parameters and through a parameter-conditioned autoregressive model that allows for temporal extrapolation beyond the training window. Gaussian processes are sampled jointly and pathwise via Matheron conditioning, ensuring that each predictive realization carries uncertainty quantification consistent with the posterior distribution. The method is tested on four parametric examples where the parameter values and the prediction horizon lie outside the training data: the two-dimensional anisotropic Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation in a time-periodic and a travelling-wave regime, each parametrised by one of its two coefficients; flow past a cylinder parametrised by the Reynolds number; and flow past an elliptic obstacle parametrised by its semi-axes. In all cases, SPOD-GPR reduces the normalised mean absolute error compared to a POD-GPR baseline, and improves the calibration of the predictive uncertainty, especially in the fluid flow cases, where POD-GPR is severely overconfident. This opens the way to spectral, uncertainty-aware reduced-order models for many-query and real-time applications, such as digital twins.

papers.title: Scalable Bayesian Optimization for Efficient Exploration of Moire Patterns
papers.abstract: Large materials design spaces often contain rare high-performing configurations that are difficult to identify through trial-and-error exploration or purely representative machine-learning (ML) sampling. In this work, we present FruBO, a flexible Bayesian Optimization framework for accelerating the discovery of optimal configurations in computationally demanding materials design problems. As a case study, we investigate multilayer Moiré patterns generated by the superposition of six rotated hexagonal lattices, where the objective is to identify the rotational conformation that maximizes pore-size uniformity, quantified using the Jain fairness index. The resulting benchmark contains 600,000 unique configurations and exhibits a highly skewed objective distribution, making the global optimum difficult to locate by random sampling. We compare random exploration, Gaussian Process-based Bayesian Optimization, and Bayesian Optimization using a lightweight CatBoost surrogate with committee-based uncertainty estimation. Random sampling identifies the global optimum only after 533,012 evaluations, requiring approximately 31 hours, while Gaussian Process-based BO becomes impractical due to GPU memory exhaustion after 290 acquired samples. In contrast, FruBO with CatBoost identifies the global optimum after 1,470 acquired samples and approximately 1.15 hours. These results demonstrate that scalable surrogate models can substantially improve the feasibility and efficiency of BO in large nanomaterials design spaces.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction for Multi-Step Forecasting: Conditional Coverage and Sharp Score Calibration Rates
papers.abstract: Uncertainty quantification in prediction is a central problem in statistics and machine learning. Conformal prediction provides a flexible approach to constructing prediction sets with valid marginal coverage under exchangeability. In this paper, we investigate conformal prediction for both one-step and multi-step forecasting from a single stationary time series, addressing temporal dependence and the additional challenges of joint prediction across multiple horizons. We propose a kernel-based framework, called Time series Residual Analysis for Calibration with Kernels (TRACK), for estimating conditional quantiles of residual scores and constructing prediction sets from rolling-window forecasters. The framework accommodates heterogeneous uncertainty across horizons and accounts for dependence induced by rolling estimation, while allowing predictor memory and forecast horizons to grow with the sample size. Our finite-sample bounds quantify how temporal dependence and overlapping score windows affect calibration and coverage. We further derive bounds for conditional quantile estimation and pointwise conditional coverage discrepancy. The guarantees extend to more general predictors that admit an accurate rolling-window approximation. We also derive matching minimax bounds over classes of known score maps, clarifying how overlapping score windows affect calibration accuracy. Experimental results from simulations and applications to wind energy generation and bike sharing demand show that our methods improve regional conditional coverage while maintaining competitive interval widths.

papers.title: Online Digital Twins: Data Assimilation and Control
papers.abstract: The online assimilation of data and the application of controls are essential ingredients of the digital twin paradigm. In this paper, we formalize the online interaction between the physical process and its virtual digital representation in the setting of continuously arriving data from the physical process and a receding horizon virtual planning process, which provides the control for the physical process. Our mathematical formulation relies on a mean field representation of the data assimilation process as well as a mean field Pontryagin minimum principle for the optimal control problem. Such mean field formulations are computationally attractive because they allow for simultaneous implementation in terms of Hamiltonian interacting particle systems. A more detailed discussion is included for the ensemble Kalman-Bucy filter in combination with affine approximations of the receding horizon control laws. This paper sets out the mathematical framework, while a computational study is left for future research.

papers.title: OASIS: Optimization-Aware Subgoal Inference with Safety Constraints for Autonomous Mobile Robot Navigation
papers.abstract: Navigation in dynamic environments requires mobile robots to make progress toward their goals while respecting motion limits and avoiding surrounding obstacles. Learned subgoal policies can guide model predictive control beyond its local prediction horizon, but a geometrically suitable subgoal does not necessarily lead to a successfully solved control problem. This paper proposes OASIS, a hierarchical navigation framework that incorporates recent optimization outcomes into reinforcement learning-based subgoal generation. A high-level policy trained using Soft Actor--Critic generates local subgoals, while a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks them subject to motion limits, geometric collision-avoidance constraints, and embedded high-order control barrier function constraints. The outcomes of controller optimizations over each subgoal interval are summarized and provided to the policy at its next decision, without requiring additional optimization calls. The framework is evaluated in five navigation scenarios with static and moving obstacles, including dense interactions and sensing uncertainty. Comparisons with hierarchical and direct-goal control variants show that OASIS achieves the highest aggregate navigation success. Matched comparisons across three training seeds further show a consistent success advantage over the otherwise identical hierarchy without optimization-status input. The selected-policy comparison also shows fewer primary optimization failures with similar mean controller time.

papers.title: Trajectory Density Ratios under Weak Support: A Survey across the Sciences
papers.abstract: Many problems across the sciences compare two stochastic processes through the sequences they generate. Reinforcement learning asks what a new policy would return from the trajectories of an old one; molecular simulation asks how much more a ligand binds from samples of the unbound state; climate attribution asks how a heat wave shifted under warming; and language-model post-training asks what a deployed agent will do from logged interactions. In every case, one quantity would answer all these questions at once: the ratio of the two probability laws over their generated sequences, the trajectory density ratio. This ratio exists only under strong conditions. When one process reaches states the other cannot, the ratio does not exist; when their overlap is thin, its variance grows without control with the sequence length; and when they concentrate on different lower-dimensional sets, the ratio is undefined altogether. Weak support of this kind is the norm for sequence data, not a sampling accident, and its price is paid in identifiability rather than in noise alone. This survey organizes the field around a three-level diagnosis of weak support and a map of the nine retreats that methods take when the full ratio is out of reach, from direct estimation and reweighting through staged decomposition, stationarization, and partial-identification bounds to smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional. Each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers and pays for the rest, and each application domain has standardized the retreat its data force. The survey closes with open problems: testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.

papers.title: Constrained Variational Policy Optimization for Hybrid Action Spaces
papers.abstract: Constrained reinforcement learning in hybrid action spaces must coordinate discrete modes and mode-conditioned continuous controls under long-horizon cost constraints. Existing constrained hybrid-action methods typically optimize factorized policies directly in parameter space, whereas Constrained Variational Policy Optimization (CVPO) separates nonparametric improvement from parametric projection in its original continuous-action formulation. We introduce Hybrid Constrained Variational Policy Optimization (H-CVPO), extending this variational framework to hybrid action spaces. Under boundedness and strict feasibility, its constrained E-step has zero duality gap and, when the dual optimum is attained at positive temperature, yields a closed-form joint target distribution over hybrid actions through exponential reward-cost reweighting. Using the exact hybrid KL decomposition, we formulate a factorized M-step that fits both policy components to this target under separate discrete and conditional-continuous trust regions. For exact E/M updates, we prove fixed-reference surrogate improvement and conditional reward-cost bounds with a sufficient feasibility-margin condition. For approximate updates, we establish the existence of a dual minimizer under continuity on a compact domain and use residual-based admissibility to determine whether to project the target. Ablations identify cost-aware reweighting as an important contributor to constraint control. Extensive experiments in simulated hybrid-control environments show that H-CVPO achieves favorable reward-cost trade-offs compared with hybrid-action baselines.

papers.title: An Evaluation of Tabular Foundation Models as Training-Free World Models
papers.abstract: World models are widely considered to be a potential key component of model-based reinforcement learning and robot planning, but typically require task-specific training on substantial interaction data. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TabFM) can serve as a training-free dynamics model for world modeling by framing next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs, and where such a model helps and where it breaks. Across synthetic dynamical systems and robot locomotion benchmarks, TabFM is more accurate than LSTM and MLP models trained from scratch on the same limited transitions in almost all settings, and among regressors fitted to the same data it is the most accurate on locomotion, while a Gaussian process is more accurate on smooth low-dimensional systems. However, models trained on the full dataset remain substantially better on most systems. When rolled out autoregressively over multiple steps, TabFM's accuracy depends strongly on how much context it is given. With a short context, its rollouts quickly degrade to the level of a trivial baseline, whereas with a long context they improve substantially and, on one locomotion task, exceed a trained LSTM. Inference is also about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM. Overall, in their current state, we find that training-free priors are useful as predictors when data are scarce and enough context is available, but they are not yet a substitute for trained world models in planning.

papers.title: LO-World: Unified BEV Latent Modeling for Joint 4D Occupancy and LiDAR Forecasting
papers.abstract: LiDAR point clouds and 3D semantic occupancy represent two distinct modalities capturing fine-grained metric geometry and dense volumetric semantics, respectively, holding natural potential for mutual complementarity. However, existing world models typically forecast these modalities independently or cascade them heuristically, missing the opportunity for reciprocal cross-modal regularization. To address this, we propose \textbf{LO-World}, a unified 4D world model that forecasts both modalities within a shared BEV latent space. This single-stream formulation enables dense semantics and metric geometry to mutually reinforce each other, while eliminating multi-pipeline redundancy. Specifically, LO-World couples an efficient hybrid range-voxel autoencoder with a flow-matching generator that caches historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LO-World outperforms prior state-of-the-art baselines, improving occupancy forecasting IoU by 10.9% and reducing LiDAR Chamfer Distance by 30.1%. Meanwhile, it sustains a real-time throughput exceeding $25$~FPS on a single RTX 4090. Our code is available at https://github.com/lzzzzzm/LO-World.

papers.title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens
papers.abstract: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.

papers.title: When Does Physics Beat Data? Data-Efficient Traffic State Estimation with Amortized PINNs
papers.abstract: Traffic state estimation (TSE) reconstructs traffic density at unmonitored locations from a sparse set of sensors. Data-driven models work well when sensors are dense but degrade sharply as coverage thins. We show that imposing the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards conservation law as a physics-informed prior makes TSE more data-efficient. On four real corridors (NGSIM, I-80, PeMS04, PeMS08), physics-informed estimators generalise to held-out sensors where data-driven models, including classical and deep kriging, overfit the observed ones. On the two shock-rich corridors the effect is a clear crossover: as more sensors are held out, data-driven models collapse while the physics-informed estimator degrades gracefully, leading the no-physics network by about 26-38% at 85-90% held out and the strongest classical kriging by about 10-21% at 90%. A matched smoothness prior does not reproduce the gain, and an extended Kalman filter on the same LWR model is outperformed on the shock corridors, so the advantage comes from how the conservation law is imposed. Finally, one loss-conditional PINN removes the per-corridor loss-weight search, matching a 20-point search at about 5x lower cost.

papers.title: Direct Trajectory Optimization for Inference-Time Alignment of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Alignment of text-to-image diffusion models with reward functions is a key challenge in controllable generation. Existing approaches typically rely on optimizing model inputs or fine-tuning denoising networks, which requires computationally expensive backpropagation through large denoising models. In this work, we propose Direct Trajectory Optimization (DTO), a training-free framework that performs alignment by directly optimizing the sampling trajectory of diffusion models. Specifically, DTO treats intermediate denoising scores and sampled noise as the optimization variables, eliminating the need for gradients through the denoising network. To mitigate the out-of-distribution problem, we introduce Reward-Optimized Score Guidance, which interpolates between the optimized scores and the pretrained model predictions to stabilize sampling, while providing a provable theoretical guarantee of reward improvement under constrained distributions. Empirically, DTO improves alignment performance across three diffusion models on two benchmarks, outperforming existing inference-time alignment methods while maintaining high efficiency. These results suggest that trajectory-level optimization is a promising direction for efficient and effective diffusion model alignment.

papers.title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity
papers.abstract: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.

papers.title: Structure-Informed Electromagnetic Feedback Control of the Vlasov-Maxwell System with Delayed Observations
papers.abstract: Feedback control of kinetic plasma instabilities is challenging because observing the full phase-space distribution is costly, while sensing and actuation inevitably introduce delay. We develop a structure-informed electromagnetic feedback framework for the Vlasov-Maxwell system that uses only macroscopic observations to control the full kinetic distribution. We first show that magnetic actuation alone does not directly regulate radial velocity moments, motivating the use of combined electric and magnetic controls. A nonlinear perturbation estimate yields an instantaneous cancellation-dissipation feedback law. To account for delayed observations, we then use Maxwell's equations to identify the macroscopic quantities governing the resulting cancellation errors, namely currents and spatial field gradients. These quantities serve as inputs to a low-rank neural operator that learns a residual correction to the delayed cancellation baseline. Thus, while the feedback depends only on low-dimensional macroscopic observables, the control objective remains the stabilization of the full distribution toward a prescribed kinetic equilibrium. Numerical experiments for two-stream and Weibel-type instabilities demonstrate effective long-time stabilization under substantial feedback delays.

papers.title: Planners Exploit Deterministic Error: Dithered Low-Bit World Models
papers.abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.

papers.title: Graph-Sparse Distributed Predictive Control for Multi-Robot Motion Planning vianEdge-Consensus ADMM
papers.abstract: This paper presents a distributed model predictive control (MPC) architecture for collision-avoiding motion planning of planar robots with double-integrator dynamics. To reduce coordination demands, a time-varying predicted conflict graph selects relevant pairwise interactions. The associated collision-avoidance constraints are convexified once per MPC update using warm-start trajectories, yielding a fixed convex quadratic program (QP). The resulting QP is then decomposed using an edge-consensus formulation of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), enabling parallel robot-local optimization and independent closed-form projections onto separating half-spaces. Execution is selectively supervised by a centralized high-order control barrier function (HOCBF) QP when the distributed candidate does not satisfy the direct-execution conditions. Evaluated in C++ simulations involving 8, 16, and 32 robots, the proposed architecture achieves collision-free execution and substantially improves computational scalability while maintaining task-level performance comparable to a centralized complete-graph baseline.

papers.title: Data-Driven Precision Control of Soft Helicoid Robots
papers.abstract: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.

papers.title: Energy-saving optimized parameters for 3D selective laser melting using dimensionless model and ANN surrogate mapping
papers.abstract: Abstract In selective laser melting (SLM), determining the optimal processing parameters, such as laser power, scanning speed, hatching space, etc., often relies on trial-and-error experiments. In this study, the final optimal parameters for SLM of Ti6Al4V were effectively characterized using the dimensionless model, melting pool geometry model, energy-saving index, and maximum hatching space. First, by combining the criteria of an optimization zone from a dimensionless model, the ratio of melting pool, and energy saving, the optimal two parameters in laser power and scanning speed were defined that not only provided excellent mechanical properties in as-built samples but also achieved a green design in manufacturing. As a result, for Ti6Al4V with the hatching space of 80 µm, an impressive relative density of 99.977% was achieved, with the tensile strength reaching approximately 1201 MPa, the yield strength reaching 1171 MPa, and the elongation rate reaching 8.2%. Subsequently, the corresponding maximum hatching space of up to 120 µm was achieved by a novel methodology proposed by our group. As a result, the energy saving was much improved to 33.4%, and the relative density of 99.948% was still held compared to the case with the hatching space of 80 µm.It is concluded that this novel approach, with an optimal parameter set in laser power and scanning speed based upon the dimensionless model, melting pool geometry, energy saving, and its corresponding maximum hatching space, can effectively minimize energy consumption and maximize throughput while still maintaining the superior mechanical qualities of the as-built samples.

papers.title: Mitigating numerical stiffness in least-squares formulations of elliptic PDEs for physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Abstract Residual-based physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) combine interior PDE and boundary residuals using mean squared errors. For elliptic boundary value problems, these formulations can show numerical stiffness causing slow training. We study a residual formulation that combines an H 0 −1 interior residual with an H 1/2 boundary residual for nonzero Dirichlet boundary data. For finite-dimensional test spaces in H 1 (Ω), we introduce two finite-dimensional approximations, the subspace-induced negative-order Sobolev seminorm (SINOS) and its dual counterpart (D-SINOS), and quantify their stiffness through a stiffness ratio defined with respect to the H 1 -norm. We establish continuity and coercivity estimates for both formulations and show that, for polynomial spaces of degree n, the stiffness ratios of SINOS and D-SINOS grow at most as O(n 2 ) and O(1), respectively. Numerical experiments recover rates of n 2.00 and n 0.05 , compared with n 6.95 and n 5.68 for MSE and L 2 -based residual losses. PINN experiments for the Poisson equation, a stationary convection-diffusion-reaction problem, and the stationary incompressible Navier-Stokes equations show that SINOS achieves consistently strong convergence and accuracy, while D-SINOS improves over MSE but does not attain the performance of SINOS. These results demonstrate that negative-order Sobolev residuals substantially reduce the stiffness of least-squares PINN formulations. At the same time, the superior PINN performance of SINOS despite the smaller stiffness ratio of D-SINOS demonstrates that stiffness mitigation alone does not determine optimization and approximation quality.

papers.title: Cost reductions in total hip arthroplasty after DRG payment reform and volume-based procurement in China: a difference-in-differences study
papers.abstract: Background: Between 2021 and 2022, China's health system reforms deployed two overlapping cost-containment instruments in quick succession: diagnosis-related group (DRG) bundled payment and a nationalized volume-based procurement (VBP) programme that cut orthopedic implant prices by 70%−90%. Disentangling their independent contributions to hospitalization costs is both methodologically challenging and policy-critical. We examined whether the January 2021 DRG roll-out in Wenzhou was associated with a differential change in total hip arthroplasty (THA) costs and adverse discharge outcomes across insurance groups, and whether the observed cost reductions are consistent with a larger contribution from either reform. Methods We analyzed 2,518 consecutive THA admissions at a tertiary hospital in Wenzhou (2015–2025). Patients were classified as Social Insurance (NRCMS, URBMI, and UEBMI; n = 2,046) or Other Payment (self-pay, full public-service, miscellaneous; n = 472). A difference-in-differences (DID) framework with year fixed effects and HC3-robust standard errors estimated the group-specific cost change associated with the reform. An event-study design assessed pre-reform parallel trends and traced the year-by-year trajectory of any post-reform divergence. Five sensitivity analyses varied the reform window (excluding 2020–2021, excluding 2021 alone, and a DRG-only window before the implant-price break), the comparison group, and the covariate set; in addition, E-values were used to assess sensitivity to unmeasured confounding. Significance was set at a two-sided α of 0.05, with Holm adjustment across the three cost outcomes. The adverse discharge outcome — defined as death, non-recovery, or other non-standard disposition at discharge — served as a safety endpoint. Results Across the full sample, median total THA cost fell from CNY 52,527 in the pre-reform period (2015–2020) to CNY 34,397 post-reform (2021–2025), a decline of 34.5%. The reduction was dominated by implant and material costs, which fell by 61.9% in Social Insurance patients (CNY 36,167 to CNY 13,772; p < 0.001) and 56.3% in Other Payment patients (CNY 36,264 to CNY 15,864; p < 0.001). The DID interaction term — capturing the group-differential change beyond the shared time trend — was not statistically significant for total cost (β = −0.015; 95% CI −0.072 to 0.042; p = 0.610), drug cost (β = −0.055; 95% CI −0.146 to 0.036; p = 0.235), or implant cost (β = −0.015; 95% CI −0.096 to 0.067; p = 0.725). Sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent: excluding 2020–2021 yielded β = −0.011 ( p = 0.760), excluding 2021 alone β = −0.014 ( p = 0.644), excluding other social insurance patients β = 0.017 ( p = 0.600), and restricting to the DRG-only window (January 2021–April 2022) β = +0.038 ( p = 0.314). The event study showed that pre-reform coefficients (2015–2019) were uniformly non-significant and centered near zero, and post-reform year estimates showed no sustained directional divergence, consistent with the absence of a large independent DRG effect over the five-year post-reform window. Adverse outcomes were rare (21 events; 0.8% overall) and did not differ differentially between groups (OR = 1.32; 95% CI 0.19–9.01; p = 0.777); this exploratory analysis was underpowered. Conclusions The similar decline in implant costs in both insurance groups, with no significant differential change in the DID analysis, is consistent with nationalized VBP being the main driver of THA cost compression in this cohort, although a DID design cannot test this directly. DRG may have contributed a modest incremental effect that this single-center design cannot isolate from the much larger procurement shock. Adverse discharge events were rare ( n = 21) and the safety analysis was underpowered, so it cannot exclude an important safety signal. These findings illustrate an evaluation challenge when supply- and demand-side reforms overlap, and point to the need for multi-site designs exploiting staggered DRG adoption to disentangle their separate contributions.

papers.title: Retrievability of Failing Zircon Dental Implant: A Case Report
papers.abstract: Background: Zirconia (Zr) dental implants have emerged as an alternative to titanium implants in implant dentistry. However, their removal can present considerable challenges because of the material's brittleness and susceptibility to fracture. This case report describes the surgical challenges encountered during the removal of a malpositioned zirconia implant and the subsequent management of the resulting bone defect. Case Presentation: This case report describes a female patient who received a Zr implant in the upper first premolar region. However, the implant was malpositioned, causing pain and pressure on the adjacent mesial tooth. A full-thickness flap was raised, and the bone was exposed. Attempts to remove the Zr implant using various techniques and tools were complicated by the implant's brittleness, which led to fracture and difficulties during removal. Ultimately, surgical removal required extensive bone removal, resulting in a significant bone defect. Fortunately, examination of the adjacent root revealed no damage due to implant misalignment. A guided bone regeneration procedure was performed to rebuild the bone defect, using platelet-rich fibrin to enhance soft tissue healing. After four months of bone graft healing, two titanium implants were placed with satisfactory primary stability. Discussion: Removal of the malpositioned zirconia implant proved challenging because of its brittleness and tendency to fracture, ultimately requiring extensive bone removal and creating a significant bone defect. Nevertheless, the adjacent tooth root remained intact. Following guided bone regeneration and a four-month healing period, the site permitted the placement of two titanium implants with satisfactory primary stability. Conclusion: This case highlights the technical challenges associated with removing malpositioned zirconia dental implants and the potential for implant fracture and substantial bone loss during retrieval. Retrieval of Zr dental implants may require specialized tools designed to accommodate the material's unique characteristics. Further research is needed to develop more effective strategies for managing Zr implant failures.

papers.title: Autogenous Tooth Sticky Bone Graft for Maxillary Radicular Cyst Defects: A Retrospective Case Series
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Radicular cysts (RCs) in the maxillary anterior aesthetic zone can cause substantial buccal bone loss and complicate implant rehabilitation. This retrospective case series evaluated autogenous tooth sticky bone (ATSB) from impacted third molars, covered with concentrated growth factor (CGF) membranes, for reconstructing these defects before delayed implant placement. Methods: Twenty patients with maxillary anterior RC-associated defects and ≥2 nonfunctional impacted third molars were treated under general anesthesia. ATSB was prepared chairside from partially demineralized dentin matrix (425–850 μm) and autogenous fibrin glue, placed after cyst enucleation, and covered with two CGF membranes. Implants were placed after 4 months. Clinical records, panoramic radiographs, and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans were reviewed. Results: The cohort comprised 12 males and 8 females (mean age, 31 years; range, 20–40). All donor and recipient sites healed uneventfully, without recorded infection or graft failure. Four-month CBCT showed increased radiopacity and trabecular-like structures within the defects. All implants achieved primary stability (implant stability quotient > 70) and showed radiographic findings consistent with osseointegration at 3 months; definitive restorations were recorded as functionally and aesthetically acceptable. Conclusions: In selected patients, ATSB with CGF membrane coverage may be a feasible option for post-enucleation reconstruction and delayed implant rehabilitation without an additional bone-harvesting site. Controlled studies with volumetric, histological, and long-term assessment are needed.

papers.title: Success of debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention for acute hematogenous periprosthetic joint infection: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Background : Acute hematogenous periprosthetic joint infection after hip or knee arthroplasty is difficult to treat. The method of debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) is widely used, but reported success rates vary, and predictors of failure remain unclear. Methods : We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase from inception through 26 November 2025 for studies reporting outcomes of DAIR in acute hematogenous periprosthetic joint infection. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. The primary outcome was pooled treatment success. Results : Forty-nine studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Reported success rates ranged from 20 % to 100 %, with a pooled success rate of 64.5 % (95 % confidence interval, 59.3 %–69.4 %; I 2 =72 %, τ 2 =0.44) in the meta-analysis. This pooled estimate describes an average across heterogeneous cohorts and should not be used as a patient-specific prediction. Success was higher in total hip arthroplasty than in total knee arthroplasty (69.4 % vs. 63.2 %). Outcomes improved over time, from 44.9 % before 2010 to 68.7 % in 2020–2025. Staphylococcus aureus infection and prolonged symptom duration before debridement were the most consistently reported predictors of treatment failure, whereas some included studies reported improved outcomes with modular component exchange. Conclusion : DAIR controls infection in about two-thirds of patients with acute hematogenous periprosthetic joint infection. Failure remains common, especially with S. aureus infection or delayed intervention, supporting early diagnosis, prompt surgery, and careful patient selection.

papers.title: A cyclic CPT-based test for soil characterization: experimental and numerical study
papers.abstract: The classical Cone Penetration Test (CPT) provides valuable information about soil strength, but does not yield directly deformability parameters. To address this limitation, a novel CPT-based testing device has been designed in the recent years to evaluate soil stiffness. The test involves a force-controlled cyclic loading applied to a penetrometer tip that moves independently from the driving shaft. In this paper, both physical experiments and a digital twin based on the Discrete Element Method (DEM) are used to evaluate the new testing method. The results demonstrate that: (1) a clearly defined pseudo-elastic behavior domain can be identified; (2) a pseudo-elastic deformation modulus can be derived; and (3) soil stiffness degradation with the stress loading level can be assessed by the test.
